title: Bell scenarios encode classical non-causality
authors: Andreas Leitherer, Kyrylo Simonov, Ravi Kunjwal, Antonio Acín, Kuntal Sengupta, Hippolyte Dourdent
abstract: Bell and contextuality scenarios are unified within the Acín-Fritz-Leverrier-Sainz hypergraph formalism, in which measurements are hyperedges. Multipartite measurements are obtained from product rules that combine independent contextuality scenarios into a single hypergraph. Several such rules exist: they are structurally distinct, yet yield the same classical, quantum, and boxworld correlations. Here, we show that this difference is not incidental, unveiling an unexpected connection. The measurements of composite Bell scenarios are exactly the process functions, the deterministic classical communication protocols that may be non-causal, i.e., lack a definite causal order without generating paradoxes. Validity of a hyperedge and logical consistency of a process function are thus one and the same condition. This allows us to characterize process functions by normalization and no-signaling alone, providing transformations that generate non-causal process functions from no-communication ones. The product rules, in turn, order process functions by causal structure, from no-communication to non-causality, which yields a graphical criterion for the latter: a process function is non-causal precisely when its hyperedge is generated by the disjunctive but not the maximal product. We thereby obtain the first joint hypergraph representation of (non-causal) process functions and (nonlocal-without-entanglement) measurements, recasting classical non-causality as a non-standard way of composing black boxes.
summary: This work develops a hypergraph formalism to unify contextuality and Bell nonlocality, extending the analysis to classical process functions. It shows that the structure of these processes directly encodes causality, providing a mathematical criterion to distinguish non-causal correlations from standard causal ones. This offers a novel, joint representation of non-causal classical correlations and nonlocal measurements.
main_problem: The paper unifies Bell and contextuality scenarios within the AFLS hypergraph formalism to characterize classical non-causality in multipartite measurements.
main_result: It establishes that the measurements of composite Bell scenarios are equivalent to process functions, and non-causality is precisely characterized by the hyperedge generated by the disjunctive but not the maximal Foulis-Randall product.
method: The authors use the AFLS hypergraph formalism, comparing different Foulis-Randall product rules (minimal, common, maximal, disjunctive) to model the composition of independent contextuality scenarios.
model_or_system: The model involves hypergraphs where vertices are outcomes and hyperedges represent measurements. The focus extends to process functions, which are deterministic classical analogues of process matrices describing single-round, deterministic classical processes among parties.
key_observables: Contextuality, Bell nonlocality, and the logical consistency of process functions (i.e., absence of causal paradoxes).
important_parameters: The structure of the Foulis-Randall product (minimal, common, maximal, disjunctive) dictates the causal structure.
main_assumptions: The equivalence between the validity of a hyperedge and the logical consistency of a process function is a central assumption used to characterize non-causality.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the AFLS hypergraph framework, comparing the naive Cartesian product to the required structure for no-signaling using the FR product, and showing the hierarchy of causal constraints.
paper_structure: The paper builds from the AFLS hypergraph formalism for contextuality, introduces the Foulis-Randall product for composition, and then maps this structure onto process functions, culminating in the characterization of non-causality via the disjunctive product.
why_interesting: While the core topic is quantum foundations (Bell tests, causality), the rigorous mathematical framework involving hypergraphs and process matrices provides powerful tools for analyzing constraints in complex quantum information protocols, which can inform open quantum systems modeling.

FIG. 2. The Cartesian product of two local contextuality scenarios leads to signaling. Two unipartite Bell scenarios HA and HB, defined by two measurements settings each hav- ing two outcomes, are composed via the Cartesian product HA × HB = (VA × VB, E(HA) × E(HB)). One can define a deterministic probabilistic model compatible with the global hypergraph (the probabilities assigned to the vertices are in- dicated in light red) such that the marginal outcome proba- bilities for A depend on the measurement setting of B. This is the case, for instance, in the first row for outcome 0 and setting 0 for A.
